definitions: Barbados played Grenada in a 1994 Caribbean Cup qualifier.
Contemporary reported event; not the final tournament or an elimination final.
Barbados needed a victory by at least two goals to qualify; a one-goal victory would leave Grenada qualifying.
Contemporary reported constraint plus arithmetic from compiled group results; qualifier goal difference, not double match points.
Late in normal time Barbados led2–1; the match later stood2–2 before extra time.
Agreement on scores; scorer and exact minute of the earlier2–1 are excluded.
A draw at full time led to sudden-death extra time; an extra-time winner gave a two-goal winning margin through double weighting.
Applicable historical rule reconstructed from contemporary description and result note; no original rulebook inspected. Not all football golden goals count double.
Barbados deliberately scored into their own net to equalize and try to reach advantageous extra time.
Contemporary report describes exchanged passes then intentional finish; motives reconstructed from reported constraint and action. No invented dialogue.
At2–2 before full time, scoring into either goal would allow Grenada to qualify: win the match, or lose by only one.
Reliable reconstruction combining contemporary reported own-goal attempt and independently recomputed qualification logic; this incentive is limited to normal time.
Barbados defended both their own goal and Grenada's goal, keeping the score2–2 until full time.

Contemporary report explicitly documents defending the opponents' goal and Grenada failing at either end; own-goal defense is consistent normal play and later detailed account. Exact player allocation/choreography is not established.
Barbados scored the extra-time winner, received the required two-goal margin and qualified.
Contemporary report plus compiled group winner. Qualification is distinct from eventual CaribbeanCup championship; no trophy or tournament-win implication.
The deliberate equalizer opened a different route to qualification: preserve a tie then score one double-weighted extra-time goal.
Later causal interpretation grounded in the actual rule and arithmetic; no optimality, safety or numerical probability claim.
Grenada's scorer made the earlier2–1 at exactly83minutes.
Contemporary Times says a Bajan own goal; later accounts differ. Scorer and exact minute excluded, without declaring which account is correct.
Exactly half Barbados's players defended each goal in specified positions.
Later analytical account gives half; contemporary report does not establish exact arrangement. Not needed for core story; exclude.
FIFA formally ruled the team blameless and abolished the rule immediately.
No inspected primary ruling or rule-amendment record; later accounts vary on timing. Exclude.
lines: Barbados scored an own goal on purpose. Then they defended both goals.
It was a Caribbean Cup qualifier in 1994. And winning the match wasn't enough.
Barbados needed to win by two goals to qualify. Late in the game, they led two-one. A win—but still elimination.
They could try to score again. Or exploit an unusual rule.
A draw at full time meant extra time. The first goal there would end the match—and count double.
So, one goal in extra time could give Barbados the two-goal margin they needed.
They deliberately scored into their own net. Two-two. Now they just needed to keep it tied.
But Grenada had spotted a way to stop them.
Score against Barbados, and Grenada wins. Score into their own goal, and Grenada loses by only one—still enough to qualify.
Before full time, either goal would do.
Barbados had to protect their own goal—and Grenada's. The opponent's net had become something they needed to defend.
They kept it two-two until full time.
Then Barbados scored the extra-time winner. It counted as a two-goal victory. They qualified.
Scoring against themselves hadn't been the mistake. It was their way of making the rules work for them.
